title: Oddworld: New 'n' Tasty
text: This is how you do a remake! The original was quite possibly the greatest 2D platformer of the late '90s, not to mention one of my favorite games of all time.  It was an odd duck, to be sure, but it executed every weird concept it presented with startling finesse, quickly cementing its cult status.  Abe the Mudokon couldn't fight one-on-one, or take more than a single blow before dying.  He was clumsy, fragile, flatulent, and so naive that he thought the slave position he was born into "a good job" -- until he discovered that the meat processing plant he labored for would soon be turning his species into an exciting new line of processed meat-pops.  This revelation launched Abe on an adventure full of open-ended puzzles, daring rescues of fellow Mudokons, and stealthy escapes.  What everybody remembers the most about the gameplay, though, was Abe's awesome ability to spiritually possess the gun-toting Slig guards, sending them on murderous rampages among their own kind, or using them to solve puzzles, and then exploding them into meaty chunks when their usefulness was done (whereupon Abe always emitted a chuckle as chilling as it was goofy).  I won't go into great detail regarding the setting, but the blackly humorous milieu of Oddworld earned the game just as much attention as its fine and varied mechanics; it succeeded handily as a not-too-preachy satire of corporate greed, but went further, becoming a fully fledged science-fantasy world that we all wanted to explore. takes everything we Oddworld fans adored about the now fuzzy-looking (but still eminently playable) classic and makes it for a whole new gaming generation.  All the classic gameplay is there, even more fun now than I remember, and what mechanical changes have been made are in the way of improvement.  Most notably, the modular movement of the original (every discrete button press resulting in a perfectly measurable step, etc.) has been replaced with a more organically flowing system; it initially makes things a little tough for even veterans, since an accidental twitch of the stick can make Abe jab his toe into a mine, but it results in a player-character who feels as alive as the person gripping the controller.  Having to take a little extra time in mastering Abe's lifelike inertia intensified my connection to the Mudokon savior, and in turn fed my sense of immersion into Oddworld at large.  But for those who absolutely can't make the leap to organic motion (and I highly recommend you try), JAW has graciously inserted a "classic" movement option. Graphically and aurally, this has to be the best remake I've ever seen; the in-game assets are so impressive that they outstrip the (quite impressive) cutscenes.  From the redneck-ish muttering of the Sligs to the posturing of the feral beasts to the mechanical rumble and blood-spattered steel of Rupture Farms itself, no game in the too-long dormant Oddworld series evokes such a strong sense of place.  Lorne Lanning and company are deeply passionate about their bizarre alternate universe and know just how to make it come alive! TLDR:  Classic gameplay and setting + new organic movement system + top-notch graphics & sound = game that you should definitely play unless amazing puzzle-platformers give you seeping hives

title: Oddworld: New 'n' Tasty
text: I'm writing this now so I can convince some of you to buy it while it's on sale. Because you should buy it no matter what. If this isn't a love letter to not only the original developers, but to the dedicated ODD fans worldwide, I don't know what is. This reimagining is so beautiful it is astounding. I'll admit I had my doubts about all of the hype, growing up with the Oddworld franchise I really didn't expect an HD remodeling of the entire game to be so impressive. I ate my expectations with sriracha. I choked it down. Not only do they lovingly keep the original storyline, they added even depth to it all. The characters, the atmosphere, the lore. All of it feels so rich and a wonder to explore. The levels are completely redone from the ground up and you can tell how much effort went into each reimagined design. Many of the original puzzles and set peices are kept, while others have multiple tweaks and additions. The original '97 title gave you 99 Mudokons to save or kill. This title gives you 300 Mudokons to save or kill. That should give you a little idea on how much extra content JAW has put into this game. They added difficulty settings: Easy, Normal and Hard - being the closest to the original. They added new mechanics such as throwing bottle caps and flint rocks for distraction/puzzle solving and changing the control scheme to fit the feel better - I.E., mainly changing your move button to the analog stick for a constant run. Oldschool Oddites need not worry, for to slow down and get to hoppin' like back in the day. Support the Dev's and they will continue to release ODD content, which is absolutely wonderful. Personal Rating: 12/10

He has his own game, Styx Master of Shadows, which is really quite good, possibly better than this one because it draws you in, and this one doesn't have a lot going for it in that department. title: Offworld Trading Company
text: My roommate walked in and asked what I was playing. I told him it was Offworld Trading Company, an RTS about building a corporation on Mars, expanding your base, and specializing in the production of a whole host of materials to earn enough money to buy out your opponents. He told me it looked pretty interesting, but mentioned that I was losing... And I was, BADLY. The match was down to myself and one other company, but that enemy had bought out two other players. They were an unstoppable behemoth with 10x the iron mines, steel mills, glass factories, electronic depots, and every other profitable thing you can imagine. It was this sort of scenerio I might have just given up and quit in any other strategy game. But, I couldn't embaress myself, here. I had an offworld market, capable of launching rockets filled with my most precious materials to the skies and bringing back buckets of cash and my opponent didn't. I coud see the flashing, red percentage next to my enemy's name, noting how close they were to buying me out. I managed to buy a bit of my enemy's stock. But, it was still going to cost 2 million to win. I sold EVERYTHING, making a little bit here, a little bit there. I looked to the right: 70%, 80%, 90%... 99%. That's it! 2 million!!! Buy, buy, buy. I won. What. I've read some reviews where people don't seem to understand why prices go up or down and don't understand some of the core mechanics of the game, so I just wanted to clear a few things up. There are 2-8 companies in each match, with a colony at the center. All goods start at a certain price. If players buy more of one resource, it goes up in price. If they sell a lot, it goes down. The colony also expands as the game goes on and each building they create has specific demands that also affect the market prices. Each player chooses one of four types of headquarters, each with their own abilities. The game is based on isometric tiles and when you start the game, you'll only have a few claims to own the tiles you choose. By leveling up your base from level 1 to level 5, you get more claims to diversify and increase production. At max level, you can build an offworld market that launches rockets into space. This secondary market isn't affected by supply and demand, it just has permanatly high prices. This makes it a very lucridive end game to reach and pile up enough money to buy out your opponents. The game is a tense, corporate competition that has so many ways to play, allowing you to build a vast mining corporation, an electronic manufacturing titan, or a chemical lab empire. You can upgrade everything, specialize or diversify, build quick and unstable, or slow and steady; the game offers a ton of ways to replay. This is a fantastic strategy game that isn't much like any major game out there and is tons of fun with friends. The AI is pretty tough, though.

title: Offworld Trading Company
text: tl/dr: Good strategy game if you want to do shorter skirmishes (30-40min each), campaign mode is a little short, but daily challenges make up for it. Pros: - Well built random map generator, provides some flexibility in strategies you can use - Resource Pricing has a nice stock market rapid price changing model - Super pretty isometric visuals - Campaign Mode introduces additional character bonuses that make for some interesting end-campaign builds - Interesting daily challenges that give you a better idea of how good you are, without having to wait to be on specific hours to get enough folks for larger multiplayer games. Cons: - Campaign mode is a little short... it's good just short... (the DLC makes this less of an issue adding a 2nd 'planet' for some increased variety) - In game time feels a tad unbalanced... Missions/Skirmishes feel "slow" at the very beginning, but last few minutes the action is almost too fast Note: I initially got this game early in Early Access - review updated for full release thoughts

title: Offworld Trading Company
text: =early access review= (beta 9) This game was a sleeper surprise for me.  I didn't expect to enjoy it as much as I have been for the last eight hours.  The concept is pretty interesting, take your average RTS and remove 'combat' from it, replacing it with rampant capitalism.  You find this shift greatly changes the nature of the game.  It's not quite like those economic space trader games, and it's not like a RTS.  Instead it's a game that really seems to sit in it's own unique subgenre. I enjoyed it quite a bit, and reminded myself that the game is still in beta whenever I found a flaw I didn't like, but honestly they weren't that big.  There were two notable cons to this game in my opinion.  The first is that the computer's voice is basically all of those crappy text to speach voices that you hear in different Operating Systems.  Some minimal voice acting to replace it would go a very very long way. The second problem I had with this game was it's price point.  $40 is a bit on the high side, and I grabbed it for $20 on a steam sale.  But even then the depth of the game feels a tiny bit shallow and repetitive for a $40 price tag.  Still if bought on sale, or if the game is expanded further during beta, I'd absolutely recommend this game for anyone who is intrigued by the concept. I look forwards to playing the game more when it is finished.

In this profane, borderline obscene all-text game, your character awakens, feeling lousy, and remembers that the day is to be spent at a local amusement park. As you prepare for the day, you are given one, two or three options (if you aren’t already crushed by a jet engine, that is.) title: One Way To Die: Steam Edition
text: My playtime: 2.5h (based on steam) *I received the Deluxe Upgrade for free One Way To Die: Steam Edition is an interactive fiction about dying. There are a bunch of text explaining the story and there will be always several options to choose with randomized results after that. The story in this game is very simple: it's about a man (you) who wants to go to and back to the last day opening of an amusement park. Although the choices will result in deaths or a continuation for the story, it won't affect the story that much. Most of the story is the same with just a little difference in detail or with an additional text explaining how the man dies. The game itself is pretty randomized; you can die without even doing anything. Any choice you choose will result in death or not based on your luck. Although you can choose which result do you want if you buy the deluxe edition (and some achievement will only unlock with the deluxe edition), that will beat the purpose of the game. Sometimes, you'll be a saboteur, the one who'll set up traps to make more deaths on the choices. There is also a counter-measure team for that, who'll disarm the traps. Whether you'll be the saboteur, the non-saboteur, or the one who disarm the trap is randomized. The music is annoying. I have to mute the game in order to play it because it's terrible. I can't really say much about the graphics because the game is just about a bunch of a text in a screen. It won't really matter for me if it's just a black and white in cmd style. At least the menu isn't hard to learn and the text is readable. Pros: - Multiple choices Cons: - Randomized results It's just an interactive fiction with a lot of reused text between the scenes. Although there are multiple choices, the choice will either be death or survive; making the choice not even useful at all.

title: Order of Battle: World War II
text: OVERALL 8/10 (as of June 2015) One just cannot resist the temptation and compare Order of Battle: Pacific to Panzer Corps even if that would not be entirely fair as "Pacific" is a beast on its own and should not be seen as a mere expansion of its illustrious predecessor. It is a "simple" wargame as Panzer Corps and uses pretty much the similar approach in terms of movement, core force build up, and, obviously, combat. So, if you enjoyed Panzer Corps, you will like this one as well. PROS: There are some serious improvements over "that" game: + Experienced units have advantages, yes, but nothing too overboard, so forget about killing off a horde of enemies with a single 5 stars Tiger tank. + Supply! oh yes, supply is very well done in this game, almost its finest point. You don't just need a clear line to be in supply, but also enough supply to keep your units up and running. + Air and Naval combat is vastly improved (yet still very simplified). + Units have several distinct abilities that make all of them useful at some point (not just limited to engineers building bridges, but also commandos not needing supply, some tanks hunkering down and so on). + The AI does a decent job at hunting down weakened units and is not an utter fool when on the attack. + Maps are detailed and terrain is critical to plan ahead + Some unique events happen during scenarios that force the player to change its strategy along the way, making it for a more dynamic experience. CONS - The hypotetical scenarios (like, invading Tokio by sea) are a bit too unrealistic. - Unit balance is not there yet: Japan built 300 tanks during the entire war, mainly deployed in mainland China. Considering each tank "unit" represent a number of tanks (how many, we don't know) I'm positive I've destroyed three times the entire Japanese WW2 tank production in 12 battles. - Some units are in dire need of an overhaul: you just cannot reload torpedoes on torpedo bombers while flying (plus Devastators were a total disaster, as Midway showed). - The nice "dynamic path" (one scenario outcome changing the next scenario that was so critical in Panzer Corps) is gone, now everything is very linear. - Commanders are far and few in between, allowing for little diversification. The potential is there for a great platform to be used for pretty much any scenario from 1940 to 1977, some game mechanics are really nice, and most of the things that need ironing (an "undo" button, unit balance, a way to get rid of the animation, magically reloading torpedo bombers in the middle of the ocean, AI constantly attacking infantry entranched in the jungle and so on) COULD be easily fixed (if there's a will to do so). All in all this could become a standard for simple wargames with very minor changes. I would not suggest the DLC way to expand it as everything important about WW2 in the Pacific is already here, but I could definitely see the same platform used to cover the Mediterrean in WW2 (pretty much absent in the 200 scenarios of Panzer Corps), Korea, 'Nam.

title: Order of Battle: World War II
text: Don't read, just go buy it. You're still here? Ok, let's talk about OoB:P. It's simply the best example of a Panzer General-type game since the original (and it may be better than those revered titles). The game is rock-solid and the production values are high (love seeing the troop animations when fighting). But that's not what makes this beer-and-pretzel wargame great. There's three things going for OoB:P that make it the gem it is. (1) Combined warfare - sea, air and land. There are so very few games that combine all 3 of these together into a workable package. Most games of this type focus on Barbarossa or Normandy where your Navy has no real application. OoB:P's focus on the Pacific allows them to focus on all 3 and they do this very well. Some scenarios are navy/air only and some are land/air only but most incorporate all 3 into one large package. As such it offers you some wonderful opportunities to work some combined arms scenarios which other games of its ilk do not. (2) Units - Not too many and not too few. Some games have an overwhelming number of units where it's difficult for the player to keep up. Others have very few units where the game is too limited. This game has a pretty fair number of units and thus you can select the ones that work with your style. My inability to effectively use anti-tank units correctly mans that I don't have to deal with those and instead I can use heavy infantry or light tanks. (3) Scenario Construction - I saved the best for last. Dear Reader, you probably already know there are many games that play similarly to OoB:P. Panzer Corps, for one, is widely recognized as a very good game. In my opinion, this is where OoB:P beats the competition. I always had a difficult time in PC because I felt the maps were too small for the number of units present. The game turns into a giant slugfest with no room for manuever and thus the scenarios become very much a puzzle and less strategic. Conversely, OoB:P's maps are quite large and there's room to move. The opportunity to flank and even attempt wide encirclements are possible. I have yet to play a scenario that felt constricting. It's the careful crafting of the scenarios that make OoB:P the great game it is. The only real complaints from my standpoint is the lack of a branching campaign structure and no voice-overs to introduce the scenario (boring text). Simply put, go look at the hours played in the other reviews. It's not uncommon to see 100 or 200 hours played and thus the game represents a massive value for your money. I'm currently over 20 and I'm not even done with the first campaign. I could easily see myself putting in 100 hours into this great game. So if you're still reading, it's time to get off the pot - go buy this one because you won't regret it. The price may be higher than other games but what's another few bucks if you get double or triple the value (and gaming time) out of it?

title: Order of Battle: World War II
text: Excellent turn-based tactical 4X game. A pure successor of good old Panzer General. First I was impressed by Panzer Corps (from the same studio), while OoB is topping it with its resource management for the troops. Now you have to keep an eye on your zone of control, otherwise, fast counterattack my cut off your supplies and then your troops may be destroyed easily. As for the 'free' World War II basic version. Some call it a demo, most players call it the intensive introduction of the whole gameplay. You are offered complete unique sandbox campaign to learn all that is necessary. Besides you can play first mission of all currently available DLC campaigns. All for free I enjoy free stuff for hours now...and do get a hunger for more. So, if you like games like Panzer General or Battle Isle, grab this little gem for free. If you like what you get, it's up to you if you buy the well-designed DLC campaigns.

text: FIrst thing to make clear, the reason I don't recommend this game has nothing to do with how much free content there is or what the DLC costs. There are enough free maps that you can determine whether this game is right for you without paying anything. As a Panzer General fan, I'm sorry to say that Order of Battle didn't offer much advantage over Panzer General or its sequels.  It also has a few drawbacks that ruin the experience for me. It isn't clear to me why certain units are pretty much useless, such as the sub. In fact naval combat overall is poorly done. I have read that there are no weather effects. I'm not sure of that because I only played the free maps, but they didn't include weather effects. If this is true, then why does this game exist - less features than a game from many years ago.

text: A game I would really appreciate a 'meh' option.  While the basic play is good, the strategy is there, supply lines are a good touch (though it's not entirely clear how supply lines work). Ground combat is decent.  Air combat is acceptable, though uninspired. Sea combat however is aggrivating to the extreme.  Routinely you can have a full strength Cruiser attack a destroyer at barely 10% and do no damage, yet said destroyer can wreck your forces. The sea combat tutorial is far from a training session, it's a full fledged combat misson with no real instructions, just a lot more ships than you have and a serious desire to take you down.  I started with 12 ships, first turn the enemy attacked me with 7 from one direction and 4 from another. And this is only a fraction of their forces. The developer clearly thinks being vastly overmatched -and- outnumbered is a good definition of 'challenging'.  I gave up after being overwhelmed twice.

title: Order of Battle: World War II
text: A very good re-make of the classic Pacific General, even though the scenarios are a bit different. There's some differences in rules as well, so it's not a plain re-make as such. But if you're looking for a game that resembles the old classics in the Generals series made by SSI, this is a very good choice. What from beginning was a game centered around the pacific war has also evolved to become centered around World War 2, so I'm expecting that with the base game, you'll be able to pick up DLCs in the future that will span over all parts of the war, not just the pacific. In fairness, this is a nische game though, more for the strategy gamers, but it has some streamlining compared to the old General series, that make it a good game for those who want to try out a strategy game as well. Somewhat high priced modules (DLCs) reduce the overall recommendation of this game, but still a recommended game for anyone looking for a remake of the old Pacific/Panzer General.

title: Order of Battle: World War II
text: Excellent game IMO. Far deeper than the Panzer Corps series which are simplified by comparison (and hence even more over-priced), which is not surprising considering they're just re-issues of Panzer/Allied General from many years ago (showing my age here). By contrast this is a much deeper, and much more rewarding game, forget just panzers and think the rest of WWII, though if you're a saddo who can't play unless he's got toy panzers, then blitzkrieg has been released just for you! I bought this for all the excellent Pacific theatre games and the Winter War DLC. The Pacific has been especially well done and there is much more use of sea and air power than in any previous game of this genre I've played. The Pearl Harbour scenarion is historically spot-on too, which bodes well for the rest of the game. Graphically it's beautiful to look at too, more importantly it's addictive to play and you'll find yourself just wanting "1 more turn" for half the night if you're not careful. It's turn based, and I find myself preffering this kind of wargame these days, much easier to control and think things through without having to click like a madman all over the screen. Grab the entire Pacific orientated DLC for a cool 40% off right now too - you'll love it. Most of the moans I've read here are actually based around the price and the cost of DLC's, well guys get used to it because it's the way all games are going like it or not. At least the devs are developing and adding to the game and giving us more of what we want. Move with the times because at the end of the day it's for them to make money... One request for the Devs; give us a British campaign in Burma - that campaign was the only one that lasted the entire war non stop, and the Japanese were still on the offensive in 1944 too. The war with Japan wasn't just in the Pacific...

title: Order of Battle: World War II
text: This is a quality turn based strategy game, it reminds me more of "Commander the great war" than of "Panzer Corps"  everyone seems to compare it to. not that it's a bad comparision, it is pretty close. it holds the same high quality as those two titles, I would say it is an over all better game, but it is a bit more in dept than these two, it is not more difficult, it's just a bit more you can do because it have more different units, you can deploy air land and sea units which gives this game a bit more content than Commander but it is just as easy to get into. I was able to play the game whitout even looking at the tutorial. there are no micro management in this game and if you are a beginner to strategy games you will probably not be disapointed. personally I would like to see a bit more micro management but the game is still very good. and even seasoned veterans would have fun. the time between turns are also very fast, it is almost instant, not at all like Commander which is a good thing. this is the best strategy game I have seen in a very long time. kudos to the developers. it is worth the full price. there is not more to say really, it's a solid game, if you are into war games you can't go wrong.

text: Not very good, the game's AI is scripted and it does terrible things that it shouldn't. I watched it several times just run away from a plane or ship with 1pt of life left when it could have destroyed it eaiily and had plenty of life to do it and take the hits it would have taken and does take anyway on the next turn. It looks and plays alot like Panzer Genarl and Panzer Corp. It just has some fundamental differences in the aftermath of battles based on what you and the AI did.

title: Order of Battle: World War II
text: The game is in no way f2p, u get a bootcamp tutorial and taster missions, which is fine if it wasnt billed as a f2p game most of my hours are from before the claimed f2p and a lot are afk hours at work so the hours a bit misleading for a thumbs down review They recently changed the core carry over rules, which was my main gripe about the game so thats good The dlc policy stays the same though, unfinsihed shoddy work, obviously rushed some even have unfinshed endings so pick your dlc carefully from the fantastic blitzkriieg to the truely dire kriegsmarine do your research for each dlc as they vary widly in quality and content Has to be a thumbs down for the game in general, even though its a massive thumbs up for a few of the dlc, blitzkrieg, morning sun, and marines
